questions.question: Fill in the blanks: **(i)** The probability of an impossible event is ______. **(ii)** The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment is called the ______. **(iii)** The probability of a certain event is ______. **(iv)** The probability of getting heads when a fair coin is tossed is ______.

solution.content: **(i)** An impossible event has no favourable outcomes, so its probability is $\frac{0}{n(S)} = 0$.
**(ii)** The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment is called the **sample space**.
**(iii)** A certain event always happens, so its probability is $\frac{n(S)}{n(S)} = 1$.
**(iv)** A fair coin has 2 equally likely outcomes, so $P(\text{heads}) = \frac{1}{2}$.

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** Probability is always a number between 0 and 1 inclusive.

questions.question: In a survey of 50 students, 15 said they like football. What is the relative frequency of students who like football?

solution.content: **Relative frequency** is the ratio of the number of favourable responses to the total number of responses: $$\text{Relative frequency} = \frac{15}{50} = \frac{3}{10} = 0.3$$

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** Relative frequency is the same as experimental probability.

questions.question: Are the following events equally likely? Give reasons. **(i)** A car starts or does not start when the key is turned. **(ii)** A fair coin shows heads or tails. **(iii)** A fair die shows 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. **(iv)** A marble drawn from a bag containing 3 red and 7 blue marbles is red or blue. **(v)** A newborn baby is a boy or a girl.

solution.content: **(i) Car starts or does not start:** **Not equally likely.** A car is much more likely to start than to fail to start, so the outcomes are not equally likely.
**(ii) Fair coin shows heads or tails:** **Yes, equally likely.** Each has probability $\frac{1}{2}$.
**(iii) Fair die shows 1–6:** **Yes, equally likely.** Each face has probability $\frac{1}{6}$.
**(iv) Red or blue marble from 3 red and 7 blue:** **Not equally likely.** $P(\text{red}) = \frac{3}{10}$ but $P(\text{blue}) = \frac{7}{10}$.
**(v) Newborn baby is a boy or a girl:** **Yes, roughly equally likely.** The chances are approximately equal (about $\frac{1}{2}$ each).

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** Outcomes are equally likely only when each has the same chance of occurring.

questions.question: Find the probability of the following events: **(i)** Getting at least one head when two coins are tossed. **(ii)** Getting an even number when a card is drawn from cards numbered 1 to 10. **(iii)** Getting a number greater than 4 when a die is rolled. **(iv)** Getting a ball that is not red when a ball is drawn from a bag containing 3 red, 2 blue and 1 green ball. **(v)** Getting exactly two heads when three coins are tossed.

solution.content: **(i) At least one head with two coins:** Sample space $S = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$, $n(S) = 4$. Favourable: $\{HH, HT, TH\}$, $n(E) = 3$. $$P = \frac{3}{4}$$
**(iii) Number greater than 4 on a die:** $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, $n(S) = 6$. Favourable: $\{5, 6\}$, $n(E) = 2$. $$P = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$$
**(iv) Not red from 3 red, 2 blue, 1 green:** Total balls $= 6$. Not red means blue or green: $2 + 1 = 3$ balls. $$P = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$$
**(v) Exactly two heads with three coins:** $S = \{HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT\}$, $n(S) = 8$. Favourable: $\{HHT, HTH, THH\}$, $n(E) = 3$. $$P = \frac{3}{8}$$

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** For 'at least one' and 'exactly' questions, always list the full sample space carefully.

questions.question: A bag contains 3 candies: one strawberry, one lemon and one mint. A candy is picked at random. What is the probability of picking the strawberry candy?

solution.content: **Sample space:** $S = \{\text{strawberry, lemon, mint}\}$, $n(S) = 3$.
**Favourable outcome:** Only 1 candy is strawberry, so $n(E) = 1$. $$P(\text{strawberry}) = \frac{1}{3}$$

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** When all outcomes are equally likely, probability is simply favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.

questions.question: Riya has 2 shirts (red and blue) and 3 pairs of pants (black, white and grey). In how many different ways can she wear a shirt and a pair of pants? List all the possible outfits.

solution.content: **Count the combinations:** For each of the 2 shirts there are 3 choices of pants, so the total number of outfits is: $$2 \times 3 = 6$$
**List all outfits:**

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** The multiplication principle: if one choice has $m$ options and another has $n$ options, together they give $m \times n$ combinations.

questions.question: A tyre company kept a record of the distance (in km) before a tyre needed to be replaced. The table shows the results of 1000 tyres. **(i)** What is the probability that a tyre will need to be replaced before 4000 km? **(ii)** What is the probability that a tyre will last more than 4000 km but less than 14000 km? **(iii)** What is the probability that a tyre will last more than 14000 km?

solution.content: **Total number of tyres:** $1000$.
**(i) Replaced before 4000 km:** 20 tyres. $$P = \frac{20}{1000} = \frac{1}{50}$$
**(ii) Lasts more than 4000 km but less than 14000 km:** $210 + 325 = 535$ tyres. $$P = \frac{535}{1000}$$
**(iii) Lasts more than 14000 km:** 445 tyres. $$P = \frac{445}{1000}$$

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** These are experimental probabilities based on the recorded data of 1000 tyres.

questions.question: The letters of the word PEACE are written on 5 cards, one letter on each card, and placed in a bag. A card is drawn at random. **(i)** What is the probability of drawing a card with the letter P, E or C? **(ii)** What is the probability of drawing a card that is not E?

solution.content: **Sample space:** $S = \{P, E, A, C, E\}$, $n(S) = 5$.
**(i) Drawing P, E or C:** The letters P, E, C appear on 4 cards (P, E, C and the second E). $$P = \frac{4}{5}$$
**(ii) Not drawing E:** The non-E cards are P, A, C — 3 cards. $$P = \frac{3}{5}$$

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** Count each card separately — the letter E appears on two cards, so it counts twice.

questions.question: A spinning arrow is on a disc with numbers 1 to 8 marked on it. Find the probability that the arrow stops on: **(i)** the number 8, **(ii)** an odd number, **(iii)** a number greater than 2, **(iv)** a number less than 9, **(v)** a multiple of 3.

solution.content: **(i) Number 8:** Only 1 outcome. $$P = \frac{1}{8}$$
**(iv) Less than 9:** All 8 numbers are less than 9. $$P = \frac{8}{8} = 1$$
**(v) Multiple of 3:** $\{3, 6\}$ — 2 outcomes. $$P = \frac{2}{8} = \frac{1}{4}$$

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** A probability of 1 means the event is certain to happen.

questions.question: A bag contains 4 red and 5 blue balls. Two balls are drawn one after the other without replacement. **(i)** Draw a tree diagram to show all possible outcomes. **(ii)** Find the probability of getting a red ball first and then a blue ball. **(iii)** Find the probability of getting two blue balls.

solution.content: **(i) Tree diagram:** First draw: Red ($\frac{4}{9}$) or Blue ($\frac{5}{9}$). After a red is drawn, 3 red and 5 blue remain (8 balls); after a blue is drawn, 4 red and 4 blue remain (8 balls).
**(ii) Red then blue:** $$P(R \text{ then } B) = \frac{4}{9} \times \frac{5}{8} = \frac{20}{72} = \frac{5}{18}$$
**(iii) Two blue balls:** $$P(B \text{ then } B) = \frac{5}{9} \times \frac{4}{8} = \frac{20}{72} = \frac{5}{18}$$

formulaBox.title: Without Replacement
formulaBox.content: After the first draw, the total number of balls decreases, so the denominator changes from 9 to 8.

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** 'Without replacement' means the first ball is not returned, so the second draw has 8 balls.

questions.question: A pair of dice is rolled. Give an example of: **(i)** an event whose probability is 0, **(ii)** an event whose probability is 1.

solution.content: **(i) Event with probability 0 (impossible event):** Getting a sum of 1 when a pair of dice is rolled. The smallest possible sum is $1 + 1 = 2$, so a sum of 1 can never occur. $$P = 0$$
**(ii) Event with probability 1 (certain event):** Getting a sum less than 13. The largest possible sum is $6 + 6 = 12$, so the sum is always less than 13. $$P = 1$$

questions.answer: (i) Getting a sum of 1 (impossible)  (ii) Getting a sum less than 13 (certain)
questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** An impossible event has probability 0 and a certain event has probability 1.

questions.question: Find the probability of the following events: **(i)** When two dice are rolled, the sum of the numbers on the dice is a prime number greater than 5. **(ii)** A bag contains 4 red, 3 green and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. The probability that the two balls are of different colours. **(iii)** Three coins are tossed. The first coin shows heads and exactly two coins show heads. **(iv)** A four-digit number is formed using the digits 1, 2, 3, 4 without repetition. The number is even. **(v)** An MCQ test has 3 questions, each with 4 options. A student guesses all answers. The probability that exactly 2 answers are correct.

solution.content: **(i) Two dice, sum is a prime greater than 5:** Total outcomes $n(S) = 36$. Prime numbers greater than 5 are 7 and 11. Sum 7: $(1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1)$ — 6 outcomes. Sum 11: $(5,6),(6,5)$ — 2 outcomes. Favourable $= 6 + 2 = 8$. $$P = \frac{8}{36} = \frac{2}{9}$$

**(ii) Two balls of different colours from 4 red, 3 green, 2 blue (without replacement):** Total outcomes: $9 \times 8 = 72$. Favourable (different colours) $= 72 - \text{(same colour)}$. Same colour: $RR = 4 \times 3 = 12$, $GG = 3 \times 2 = 6$, $BB = 2 \times 1 = 2$; total same $= 20$. Different $= 72 - 20 = 52$. $$P = \frac{52}{72} = \frac{13}{18}$$
**(iii) Three coins, first is heads and exactly two heads:** $n(S) = 8$. Favourable: $\{HHT, HTH\}$ — 2 outcomes. $$P = \frac{2}{8} = \frac{1}{4}$$

**(iv) Four-digit number from 1, 2, 3, 4 without repetition, even:** Total numbers: $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$. For an even number, the last digit must be 2 or 4 (2 choices), then the remaining 3 digits can be arranged in $3! = 6$ ways: favourable $= 2 \times 6 = 12$. $$P = \frac{12}{24} = \frac{1}{2}$$

**(v) MCQ: 3 questions, 4 options each, exactly 2 correct:** For each question, $P(\text{correct}) = \frac{1}{4}$ and $P(\text{wrong}) = \frac{3}{4}$. Exactly 2 correct can happen in 3 ways (which question is wrong). Each way: $\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{3}{64}$. $$P = 3 \times \frac{3}{64} = \frac{9}{64}$$

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** For 'different colours', it is often easier to compute the total and subtract the 'same colour' cases.

questions.question: A box contains 4 balls numbered 1, 2, 3 and 4. Two balls are drawn. **(i)** How many outcomes are there if the first ball is put back before the second is drawn (with replacement)? **(ii)** How many outcomes are there if the first ball is not put back (without replacement)? **(iii)** What are the sizes of the sample spaces in the two cases?

solution.content: **(i) With replacement:** Each draw has 4 choices, so $4 \times 4 = 16$ outcomes.
**(ii) Without replacement:** First draw has 4 choices, second draw has 3 choices, so $4 \times 3 = 12$ outcomes.
**(iii) Sample space sizes:** With replacement: $n(S) = 16$; without replacement: $n(S) = 12$.

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** With replacement the sample space is larger because the same ball can be drawn twice.

questions.question: A coin is tossed and a card is drawn from 6 cards numbered 1 to 6. Write the sample space $S$ and find $n(S)$.

solution.content: **Sample space:** Each outcome is a pair (coin result, card number): $$S = \{(H,1), (H,2), (H,3), (H,4), (H,5), (H,6), (T,1), (T,2), (T,3), (T,4), (T,5), (T,6)\}$$
**Size of sample space:** $$n(S) = 2 \times 6 = 12$$

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** When two independent experiments are combined, multiply the number of outcomes.

questions.question: Three coins are tossed. Which of the following is the correct sample space for the number of heads? **(i)** $\{1, 2, 3\}$ **(ii)** $\{0, 1, 2\}$ **(iii)** $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ **(iv)** $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$

solution.content: **Possible number of heads when three coins are tossed:** You can get 0, 1, 2 or 3 heads.
**Check each option:** (i) $\{1, 2, 3\}$ misses 0 heads. (ii) $\{0, 1, 2\}$ misses 3 heads. (iii) $\{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$ includes 4 heads, which is impossible with 3 coins.
**Correct sample space:** $$\{0, 1, 2, 3\} \quad \text{(option iv)}$$

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** The sample space must contain every possible outcome and no impossible ones.

questions.question: A drop of dye is dropped on a rectangular sheet of paper of size 3 m by 2 m. A circle of diameter 1 m is drawn inside the rectangle. What is the probability that the drop of dye falls inside the circle?

solution.content: **Area of the rectangle:** $$A_{\text{rect}} = 3 \times 2 = 6 \text{ m}^2$$
**Area of the circle:** The diameter is 1 m, so the radius is $\frac{1}{2}$ m. $$A_{\text{circle}} = \pi r^2 = \pi \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{\pi}{4} \text{ m}^2$$
**Probability (geometric probability):** $$P = \frac{\text{Area of circle}}{\text{Area of rectangle}} = \frac{\frac{\pi}{4}}{6} = \frac{\pi}{24}$$

formulaBox.title: Geometric Probability
formulaBox.content: $$P = \frac{\text{Area of favourable region}}{\text{Area of total region}}$$

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** When outcomes are spread over a region, probability is the ratio of areas.
